prize_parts.citation: for discoveries of the physiology of glucagon-like peptide-1 and the identity of its active form, which enabled incretin-based therapies for diabetes and obesity

statement.case_for: My preferred configuration is unchanged: B025 as a stand-alone prize for Drucker, Holst and Mojsov. The case rests on the discovery chain and not on the six first places. Proglucagon processing and gut secretion (Holst), the biology of GLP-1 and the therapeutic rationale (Drucker), and the identity and synthesis of the active peptide (Mojsov) were established as physiology before any drug existed. That physiology is now confirmed by replicated randomized trials in type 2 diabetes, obesity, and cardiovascular and renal outcomes, so there is no maturity concern. Reading the full round-1 exchange, no member has produced a scientific reason to prefer another achievement. The chair's question on a second part is the one that matters. Each of the three names has a distinct, defensible claim, and I will not remove one to make room for a second achievement whose case is weaker on originality than GLP-1.
statement.case_against: The open weakness is attribution and the committee should say so openly in its citation work. Priority for the active GLP-1(7-36) peptide is contested, Habener is outside the credited names, and Knudsen's acylated analogues are what turned the physiology into drugs, yet she would be left out. None of the five colleagues has changed my view that this is a limit on the configuration and not a reason to defer: the citation can name the physiology and the identity of the active form and mention incretin-based therapies without claiming priority beyond what the evidence supports. A second concern remains that the scale of the commercial success may make the prize look like a verdict on a drug class and not on the underlying science. I cannot verify the historical priority record from the material supplied, and I do not pretend to.

responses.point: Linnarsson moved from Drucker, Holst and Knudsen to Drucker, Holst and Mojsov, keeping Knudsen's analogues as a reservation to be told in the citation, and he asked me whether the cytokine biology behind TNF blockade is covered by Feldmann and Maini.
responses.response: You asked a fair question on B031 and my answer is only partly yes. Feldmann and Maini are credited for the step that matters most, showing in patients that blocking a single cytokine could control chronic inflammation, and the finding that TNF dominates the cytokine cascade in rheumatoid synovium came from Feldmann's laboratory. TNF itself and the antibody engineering sit with others, so the pair covers the clinical and mechanistic proof and not the whole biology. That is exactly why I now treat B031 as an alternative and not as a rival to B025. On Knudsen I agree with your move: I would put the therapeutic arm in the citation wording and keep her as the first name to revisit, but only if the committee decides the prize should reward the drug step.

responses.point: Perlmann argues that TNF blockade is clinical proof of concept closer to development than to a new biological principle, that Lasker recognition already covers it, and that UPR should rank above it because a new signalling logic was found.
responses.response: I accept part of this. The identification of TNF as the master regulator in the rheumatoid cytokine network was a mechanistic finding and not only a trial, but I agree it is less of a new principle than the organelle-to-nucleus signalling logic of UPR, and a Lasker award does not decide the matter either way. Your argument moves me on B045: I now list it as an alternative, replacing B051, because your point on the missing Eshhar credit in CAR-T is stronger than my earlier treatment of it. I still hold that PERK and ATF6 complicate a Walter and Mori pair, so the citation would have to be limited to the Ire1/Hac1 (XBP1) arm. I also agree with you that priority evidence on Mojsov and Habener should be examined before the final ballot and not assumed.

responses.point: The chair holds that B045 has the cleanest attribution on the list, that its still-developing disease translation is a reason for patience and not a flaw, and asks whether a second achievement should share the prize with B025.
responses.response: On your direct question, I do not support a second achievement sharing the prize with B025 this year. It would force one of Drucker, Holst or Mojsov out, and I find no scientific reason for that. Your point on patience for B045 is well taken and I have softened my earlier clinical objection: for a conceptual discovery, delayed translation does not lower its standing, and I would no longer rank it behind the immunotherapies on that basis alone. I would still ask that its citation avoid implying that the whole UPR is attributed to two people. Where I stay different from you is B050, which I keep below the others because of the six-name allocation problem; I see no trio of Bamberg, Nagel, Hegemann, Boyden, Deisseroth and Miesenböck that does not leave out a strong claimant.

responses.point: Sandberg reads TNF blockade as translation of earlier cytokine biology, ranked it last, and describes CAR-T as the stronger clinical case, with B045 as the cleaner configuration.
responses.response: I agree that B045 is cleaner and CAR-T has the stronger clinical record, and your formulation helped me, because the two objections point in different directions and neither is decisive alone. Where I differ is that I do not think the translation label fully applies to TNF: the demonstration that one cytokine drives chronic inflammation changed how autoimmune disease is classified, which is more than a clinical proof of concept. I also accept your caution that it enters a prize only if a GLP-1 name is dropped, so it cannot be part of my configuration. Between your two alternatives, I now rate B045 above B051 because Eshhar's absence leaves the conceptual origin of CAR-T outside the names, while solid-tumour efficacy and toxicity remain open.

responses.point: El Manira holds that the contested peptide priority should be handled in the citation and not used as a reason to defer, and that a method such as optogenetics is a transformative tool but not yet a settled attribution.
responses.response: I agree with the first point and I have drafted the citation with that in mind: it speaks of the identity of the active form and does not assert who was first. On optogenetics, your own proposal of Deisseroth, Hegemann and Nagel continues to show the problem, since it omits Bamberg, Boyden and Miesenböck. Nobel precedent shows methods can be honoured, so I do not reject it as a category, but I cannot support it while the allocation is unresolved, and I note that you also did not move it into your preferred configuration.

uncertainties: Whether the priority record for the active GLP-1 peptide supports Mojsov over Habener and others, which I cannot settle from the supplied evidence.
Whether the committee wants a physiology-centred citation for B025 or a therapeutic one, which would revive Knudsen's place.
How a B045 citation could be limited to the Ire1/Hac1 (XBP1) arm without understating the PERK and ATF6 branches.
How much weight the clinical proof of principle in B031 deserves against the conceptual discovery in B045, if the committee ever treats a second option as live.
statement.conflict_note: No conflict with any credited name on the shortlist. My field is autoimmunity and rheumatology, which is relevant to B031 (Feldmann and Maini, rheumatoid arthritis), but I document no personal, institutional or co-authorship tie to either and I do not infer one from shared field. My Karolinska Institutet setting is shared with other researchers and is not a tie to any credited name. No recusal is needed and I would declare any connection that emerged.
